extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in humor research, joke-writers, comedians, and cross-cultural communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirical patterns for writing jokes that score highly across large, cross-cultural online audiences (LaughLab). Focuses on accessibility, structure, protagonist sympathy, misdirection type, length, and cultural retellability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the joke universally accessible (no cultural insider knowledge)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the joke universally accessible (no cultural insider knowledge)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LaughLab found top jokes avoided culturally specific references so they could be understood by many nationalities. This criterion appears in the explicit LaughLab Working Rubric and is tied to higher cross-cultural ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could it be re-told across countries with minimal translation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Could it be re-told across countries with minimal translation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit Working Rubric item emphasizing retellability — jokes that require little localization or idiomatic phrasing travel better across cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there a sympathetically dim character?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a sympathetically dim character?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winning jokes often feature a dim character who evokes 'we laugh WITH, not AT' — the character's foibles are treated gently so the superiority feeling doesn't sting. This is explicitly in the Working Rubric and discussed in analysis of the winning joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke provide superiority WITHOUT malice?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke provide superiority WITHOUT malice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The world's funniest jokes give a 'feel good' superiority that requires no malice; the audience should feel amused rather than mean-spirited. Relevant to audience empathy and ethical acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the misdirection conceptual, not just verbal/wordplay?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the misdirection conceptual, not just verbal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working Rubric item and cross-cultural finding: top jokes rely on a conceptual twist or unexpected logic (incongruity) rather than purely on puns or language-specific wordplay, making them more translatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two stages of misdirection / unusual structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The winning joke succeeded in part because it used two sequential misdirections — a layered setup that leads audiences through one surprise and into another. This structural complexity (but still clear) can increase amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline relies on a conceptual twist, not wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: A punchline relying on a CONCEPTUAL twist, not wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-cultural universals: conceptual twists translate better than wordplay. Anti-pattern: jokes depending on puns/idioms will lose impact when translated or told to different-language audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear two-character setup
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-cross-cultural jokes often have a simple interaction between two characters, which clarifies roles and expectations and makes the twist easier to process and retell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misunderstanding rather than deception
rubrics_metrics.description: A misunderstanding rather than a deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes built on honest misunderstanding (miscommunication) rather than intentional deceit tend to be more universally liked — they preserve sympathy for the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length close to 100 words (~103 words optimal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Length: 103 words appears to be the optimal joke length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work by LaughLab shows an empirical peak around ~103 words. The Working Rubric item 'Is the joke length close to 100 words?' captures this. Guidance: neither too short to lack setup nor too long to lose attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-class theory of joke types
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes broadly cluster into: 1) Relief (sex, death, taboo), 2) Superiority (laugh at someone else's failure), 3) Incongruity (surprise at unexpected logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify jokes and craft blends: 'the world's funniest jokes pull from incongruity + a touch of superiority that doesn't sting.' Relief jokes relieve tension, superiority evokes benign amusement, incongruity relies on conceptual twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal protagonists (especially ducks) increase ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal protagonists (especially ducks) — higher ratings; possibly due to K-sound or cultural absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern observed in top-rated jokes: animal characters (ducks singled out) were overrepresented. Implication for writing: using non-human protagonists can increase absurdity and reduce interpersonal sting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience / time-of-day effects on ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day: jokes rated highest at 6pm; lowest in early morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical note indicating that when you solicit ratings or present jokes matters. For contest design or testing, consider time-of-day as a covariate affecting perceived funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific preferences (adjust for audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Country differences: Brits/Irish/Aussies preferred wordplay; Americans/Canadians preferred superiority jokes; Germans rated everything more positively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for tailoring jokes or interpreting ratings: local preferences exist though variation was smaller than expected. When targeting a specific national audience, prefer forms they historically favor (e.g., wordplay for UK audiences).
